Battle of Marathon. Near the town of Marathon, approximately 40 kilometers northeast of Athens, Greek forces faced off against invading Persian armies. The date was 490 BC, and the victory that followed would prove that the Persian Empire was not invincible.

King Darius I had sent this invasion force to punish Athens for supporting the Ionian Revolt and to expand his empire into Greece. The Athenian commander Miltiades devised tactics that exploited the terrain and the Persian weakness in close combat.

The Greeks fielded roughly 10,000 hoplites against a Persian force estimated at 20,000 to 40,000 soldiers. Despite the odds, the decisive tactic proved to be a heavy infantry phalanx charge that broke the Persian center. The Persian army routed, and their fleet retreated to Asia Minor without ever launching a landing on Greek soil.

A legend grew from this battle. A runner named Philippides supposedly ran the 40 kilometers from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory, an act that would eventually spawn the modern marathon race.

The battle became a defining moment in Athenian identity and Western history. It showed Athens that she could stand against the great powers of the world. Later, the leader Themistocles would take the lessons of Marathon and build upon them, creating Athenian naval supremacy. The victory unleashed Athenian confidence that would transform the city into the democratic powerhouse of the fifth century. And it was only the beginning of the Persian Wars, which would rage on through other clashes like Salamis, where Athenian ships would decisively defeat the Persian fleet.
